This is a 60–70-year-old long-term smoker (40 pack-years) presenting with insidious, progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough over two months — classic for chronic airflow limitation. While bronchodilator reversibility testing is pending, the clinical context strongly favors irreversibility: age, heavy smoking history, chronicity (>2 months), absence of atopy/asthma features (no nocturnal symptoms, no diurnal variation, no personal/family history of asthma or allergy), and lack of eosinophilic or allergic biomarkers. Asthma is less likely in this demographic without reversible physiology or inflammatory markers; ACOS would require evidence of both asthma and COPD features — currently absent. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is possible but rare, and would typically present earlier (<45 years) or with basilar-predominant emphysema — not yet assessed. HRCT is needed to phenotype (emphysema vs. airway-dominant), but the pretest probability of COPD is exceptionally high. No red flags (e.g., hemoptysis, weight loss, clubbing, crackles, JVD, edema) argue against ILD, HF, malignancy, or infection. Thus, pending reversibility testing — which is highly unlikely to show ≥12% *and* ≥200 mL improvement in FEV1 in this setting — the most parsimonious, evidence-based, and clinically urgent diagnosis is established COPD.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
